text.formula: Each firefly flashes at its own speed
A weak pull: still out of step
Pull harder… suddenly they flash together
The arrow is the average: long = in step

youtube.title: How fireflies fall into step (the Kuramoto model) ✨ #shorts
youtube.description:
Each one nudges its phase towards the average. Above a critical pull, order appears all at once.

presets.name: Lesson · A Sound That Rises Forever

hook.text: Does this sound ever stop rising?

text.formula: One note going up a semitone each step
Six octaves at once, loudest in the middle
After 12 steps: the same chord again

youtube.title: The Shepard scale: rising forever 🔁 #shorts
youtube.description:
The top note fades out while a new bottom note fades in, so the climb never ends.

text.formula: Three equal suns can chase each other on a figure eight
Nudge one by a hair: the ghost drifts slowly away
Masses 3, 4, 5 at rest: chaos, then one is thrown out

youtube.title: The three-body problem: a perfect figure eight and pure chaos ☀️ #shorts
youtube.description:
Found in 1993 by Moore, proved by Chenciner and Montgomery in 2000: three equal masses on one figure-eight orbit.

text.formula: A small swing: calm and regular
A big swing: wild and unpredictable
Nine start a hair apart… and then go their own way

youtube.description:
The same equations, starting angles a ten-thousandth of a radian apart: after a few seconds they disagree completely.

text.formula: Write the numbers on a square spiral
Keep only the primes: diagonal lines appear
On a round spiral the lines become curves
Gold: n² + n + 41, primes for n = 0 … 39

youtube.title: The hidden lines of the prime numbers 🔢 #shorts
youtube.description:
Ulam noticed it in 1963, doodling in a meeting: on a spiral the primes crowd onto lines.

text.formula: Four slides from the same top to the same bottom
The straight line is the shortest, but not the fastest
On a cycloid, from any height, they arrive together

youtube.title: The brachistochrone: why the fastest slide is a curve 🛝 #shorts
youtube.description:
Johann Bernoulli’s 1696 challenge: the cycloid. It is also the tautochrone: the time to the bottom does not depend on where you start.
